original_abstract: Omnidirectional scene text detection has received increasing research attention. Previous methods directly predict words or text lines of quadrilateral shapes. However, most methods neglect the significance of consistent labeling, which is important to maintain a stable training process, especially when a large amount of data are included. For the first time, we solve the problem in this paper by proposing a novel method termed Sequential-free Box Discretization (SBD). The proposed SBD first discretizes the quadrilateral box into several key edges, which contains all potential horizontal and vertical positions. In order to decode accurate vertex positions, a simple yet effective matching procedure is proposed to reconstruct the quadrilateral bounding boxes. It departs from the learning ambiguity which has a significant influence during the learning process. Exhaustive ablation studies have been conducted to quantitatively validate the effectiveness of our proposed method. More importantly, built upon SBD, we provide a detailed analysis of the impact of a collection of refinements, in the hope to inspire others to build state-of-the-art networks. Combining both SBD and these useful refinements, we achieve state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks, including ICDAR 2015, and MLT. Our method also wins the first place in text detection task of the recent ICDAR2019 Robust Reading Challenge on Reading Chinese Text on Signboard, further demonstrating its powerful generalization ability. Code is available at this https URL.
generated_abstract: Scene text detection is a fundamental component of scene text recognition, yet remains difficult because text in natural images appears at arbitrary orientations, scales, aspect ratios, and, in many cases, irregular or curved shapes. Conventional object-detection pipelines rely on proposals, aggregation, or other elaborate post-processing, while segmentation-based approaches may struggle to separate adjacent instances. We address this problem with an end-to-end detection framework that combines dense text-region prediction with direct geometric localization and an adaptive representation of text boundaries. The design is motivated by the efficiency of single-network detectors, the robustness of pixel-wise segmentation, and the ability of corner- or boundary-based regression to represent long, oriented text naturally. It is intended to detect quadrilateral as well as arbitrary-shaped text regions while retaining efficient inference and minimal post-processing. Evaluation on established benchmarks, including ICDAR2013, ICDAR2015, MSRA-TD500, COCO-Text, CTW1500, and Total-Text, is used to assess localization accuracy and runtime across focused, incidental, oriented, and curved text. The available evidence establishes these goals and evaluation dimensions, but does not determine the framework’s specific architectural innovation or quantitative results.

original_abstract: Conventional cross-domain image-to-image translation or unsupervised domain adaptation methods assume that the source domain and target domain are closely related. This neglects a practical scenario where the domain discrepancy between the source and target is excessively large. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to learn domain adaptive features between the largely-gapped source and target domains with unlabeled domain bridges. Firstly, we introduce the framework of Cycle-consistency Flow Generative Adversarial Networks (CFGAN) that utilizes domain bridges to perform image-to-image translation between two distantly distributed domains. Secondly, we propose the Prototypical Adversarial Domain Adaptation (PADA) model which utilizes unlabeled bridge domains to align feature distribution between source and target with a large discrepancy. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed models.
generated_abstract: Deep neural networks often suffer from domain shift: models trained with abundant labels in one domain can perform poorly on an unlabeled target domain whose appearance, modality, or data distribution differs. We study unsupervised domain adaptation, where knowledge must be transferred without requiring target-domain annotations. Building on representation learning, adversarial training, discrepancy minimization, and distribution-matching objectives, we consider how to learn features that remain discriminative for the source task while becoming insensitive to domain-specific variation. We further examine adaptation at multiple levels, including pixel transformations, intermediate representations, joint feature-label distributions, and task-specific decision boundaries, as well as transfer from multiple source domains and across related tasks. Our approach is designed to exploit labeled source data together with unlabeled target observations and to accommodate substantial shifts between domains. The cited results establish that aligning domains while preserving class structure is more effective than indiscriminate feature matching, and that adversarial and moment-based objectives can improve recognition across image-classification and segmentation settings. These findings support domain adaptation as a practical means of reducing annotation requirements, while leaving the precise implementation and empirical contribution of the present study unspecified by the available material.

original_abstract: The revolution in computer hardware, especially in graphics processing units and tensor processing units, has enabled significant advances in computer graphics and artificial intelligence algorithms. In addition to their many beneficial applications in daily life and business, computer-generated/manipulated images and videos can be used for malicious purposes that violate security systems, privacy, and social trust. The deepfake phenomenon and its variations enable a normal user to use his or her personal computer to easily create fake videos of anybody from a short real online video. Several countermeasures have been introduced to deal with attacks using such videos. However, most of them are targeted at certain domains and are ineffective when applied to other domains or new attacks. In this paper, we introduce a capsule network that can detect various kinds of attacks, from presentation attacks using printed images and replayed videos to attacks using fake videos created using deep learning. It uses many fewer parameters than traditional convolutional neural networks with similar performance. Moreover, we explain, for the first time ever in the literature, the theory behind the application of capsule networks to the forensics problem through detailed analysis and visualization.
generated_abstract: The rapid development of face manipulation and computer-generated imagery has made forged images and videos increasingly difficult to distinguish from authentic media, threatening digital trust and biometric authentication. Existing forensic approaches based on hand-crafted texture cues are limited, while learned detectors may overfit particular attacks, compression levels, datasets, or visual distractors. Building on convolutional feature learning for face anti-spoofing, compact forensic networks, capsule-based detection, local noise and camera characteristics, and recurrent models that exploit temporal information, we investigate robust detection of manipulated facial content. Our approach uses deep representations of facial appearance and, where available, temporal evidence, while incorporating face-specific preprocessing and information that supports discrimination under strong compression and domain mismatch. We consider prominent manipulations including DeepFakes, Face2Face, FaceSwap, and NeuralTextures, and evaluate both image- and video-based detection, with attention to localization and previously unseen attacks. The cited evidence establishes that learned features substantially outperform traditional descriptors, temporal modeling improves video detection, and domain-specific or multi-task information can improve generalization. It does not determine a more specific architecture or training protocol; consequently, our conclusions are limited to the importance of robust, attack- and domain-aware forensic learning.

original_abstract: Neural Networks trained with gradient descent are known to be susceptible to catastrophic forgetting caused by parameter shift during the training process. In the context of Neural Machine Translation (NMT) this results in poor performance on heterogeneous datasets and on sub-tasks like rare phrase translation. On the other hand, non-parametric approaches are immune to forgetting, perfectly complementing the generalization ability of NMT. However, attempts to combine non-parametric or retrieval based approaches with NMT have only been successful on narrow domains, possibly due to over-reliance on sentence level retrieval. We propose a novel n-gram level retrieval approach that relies on local phrase level similarities, allowing us to retrieve neighbors that are useful for translation even when overall sentence similarity is low. We complement this with an expressive neural network, allowing our model to extract information from the noisy retrieved context. We evaluate our semi-parametric NMT approach on a heterogeneous dataset composed of WMT, IWSLT, JRC-Acquis and OpenSubtitles, and demonstrate gains on all 4 evaluation sets. The semi-parametric nature of our approach opens the door for non-parametric domain adaptation, demonstrating strong inference-time adaptation performance on new domains without the need for any parameter updates.
generated_abstract: Neural machine translation offers fluent outputs, but often sacrifices adequacy, especially for rare words and phrases, long sentences, domain mismatch, and discourse phenomena. Encoder–decoder models alleviate the limitations of fixed-length representations through attention and soft alignment, while phrase-based statistical translation provides translation probabilities, language-model scores, and explicit phrase structure. Retrieval-based methods further improve recall by reusing translation pieces from previously seen sentence pairs. Building on these complementary strengths, we investigate an approach that combines neural decoding with phrase-based and retrieval-based evidence, using search and alignment information to guide candidate generation and selection. The design retains the fluent sequence modeling of attention-based neural translation while addressing omissions and inappropriate translations through explicit phrase-level scores or constraints. We evaluate translation quality against neural and phrase-based baselines, examining adequacy, fluency, rare-word recall, and the effect of retrieved relevance. The results show that integrating complementary signals improves neural translation, particularly when training data or neural search is insufficient, while preserving the fluency and practical decoding efficiency that motivate neural machine translation.

original_abstract: In line with recent advances in neural drug design and sensitivity prediction, we propose a novel architecture for interpretable prediction of anticancer compound sensitivity using a multimodal attention-based convolutional encoder. Our model is based on the three key pillars of drug sensitivity: compounds’ structure in the form of a SMILES sequence, gene expression profiles of tumors and prior knowledge on intracellular interactions from protein-protein interaction networks. We demonstrate that our multiscale convolutional attention-based encoder significantly outperforms a baseline model trained on Morgan fingerprints, a selection of encoders based on SMILES as well as previously reported state of the art for multimodal drug sensitivity prediction (R2 = 0.86 and RMSE = 0.89). Moreover, the explainability of our approach is demonstrated by a thorough analysis of the attention weights.
