generated_abstract: Accurate prediction of anticancer drug sensitivity is central to precision oncology, yet response depends on a complex interaction between the molecular state of a cancer cell and the properties and targets of a drug. Existing approaches have modeled genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic, and proteomic profiles, chemical structure, drug-induced expression, pathway activity, and protein-interaction information, using regression, classification, multitask learning, network-based link prediction, ensemble learning, and attention-based deep learning. Building on these advances, we investigate an integrative strategy for predicting drug–cell-line responses, representing both sides of the interaction with biologically informative molecular features and exploiting relationships among drugs, cells, targets, and pathways. We assess its ability to distinguish sensitive from resistant pairs and to estimate quantitative response values such as IC50, while examining whether the learned representations provide interpretable biological signals. The combined evidence indicates that incorporating complementary cellular and chemical information, together with biological network context and shared structure across drugs, can improve accuracy, robustness, and generalization beyond single-view models. Such predictive modeling may support prioritization of therapeutic options, estimation of unmeasured responses, drug repurposing, and mechanistic hypothesis generation.

original_abstract: The inability to generalize beyond the distribution of a training set is at the core of practical limits of machine learning. We show that the common practice of mixing and shuffling training examples when training deep neural networks is not optimal. On the opposite, partitioning the training data into non-i.i.d. subsets can serve to guide the model to rely on reliable statistical patterns while ignoring spurious correlations in the training data. We demonstrate multiple use cases where these subsets are built using unsupervised clustering, prior knowledge, or other meta-data from existing datasets. The approach is supported by recent results on a causal view of generalization, it is simple to apply, and it demonstrably improves generalization. Applied to the task of visual question answering, we obtain state-of-the-art performance on VQA-CP. We also show improvements over data augmentation using equivalent questions on GQA. Finally, we show a small improvement when training a model simultaneously on VQA v2 and Visual Genome, treating them as two distinct environments rather than one aggregated training set.
generated_abstract: Visual Question Answering (VQA) models are intended to answer questions by integrating linguistic and visual information, yet they often exploit language and unimodal priors instead of grounding predictions in image content. Because these correlations may be shared by training and test data, conventional evaluation can overestimate visual reasoning ability and obscure poor generalization to changed answer distributions. This paper examines the language-prior problem and builds on efforts to expose it through balanced data, complementary image pairs, and bias-sensitive evaluation. It further considers approaches that encourage visual grounding by disentangling visual concept recognition from answer-space prediction, adversarially suppressing question-only information, or reweighting examples according to their reliance on unimodal cues. Quantitative measures of prior reliance and regularization strategies provide additional means to assess and alleviate this behavior. Across the resulting evaluations, established VQA models experience substantial degradation when answer priors change or when complementary images require different answers, demonstrating that high conventional accuracy does not ensure image understanding. Bias-aware training improves robustness, although the evidence also indicates that reducing language priors remains challenging and must be balanced against overall VQA performance.

original_abstract: Biological evolution has distilled the experiences of many learners into the general learning algorithms of humans. Our novel meta reinforcement learning algorithm MetaGenRL is inspired by this process. MetaGenRL distills the experiences of many complex agents to meta-learn a low-complexity neural objective function that affects how future individuals will learn. Unlike recent meta-RL algorithms, MetaGenRL can generalize to new environments that are entirely different from those used for meta-training. In some cases, it even outperforms human-engineered RL algorithms. MetaGenRL uses off-policy second-order gradients during meta-training that greatly increase its sample efficiency.
generated_abstract: Designing effective learning algorithms remains laborious, requiring choices about optimization updates, losses, returns, exploration incentives, and adaptation mechanisms. We study the problem of automating this design process through meta-learning: rather than fixing these components by hand, we learn procedures that improve performance across a distribution of tasks and adapt rapidly to previously unseen problems. Building on reinforcement-learning formulations of algorithm discovery, recurrent representations of fast learning, gradient-based adaptation, learned losses, and programmatic searches over curiosity mechanisms, we view an algorithm as a trainable object whose behavior is optimized by an outer learning process. This perspective permits the learned procedure to exploit task structure, experience history, stochastic gradients, and auxiliary information while using conventional learning within individual tasks. Across reinforcement-learning and supervised-learning settings, the cited results indicate that learned algorithms can accelerate convergence, improve final performance, reduce the data required for adaptation, and generalize beyond their training tasks. They also show that such procedures may differ qualitatively from hand-designed algorithms, supporting automated algorithm design as a promising route toward more efficient and broadly transferable learning systems.

original_abstract: Reed-Muller (RM) codes are among the oldest, simplest and perhaps most ubiquitous family of codes. They are used in many areas of coding theory in both electrical engineering and computer science. Yet, many of their important properties are still under investigation. This paper covers some of the recent developments regarding the weight enumerator and the capacity-achieving properties of RM codes, as well as some of the algorithmic developments. In particular, the paper discusses the recent connections established between RM codes, thresholds of Boolean functions, polarization theory, hypercontractivity, and the techniques of approximating low weight codewords using lower degree polynomials. It then overviews some of the algorithms with performance guarantees, as well as some of the algorithms with state-of-the-art performances in practical regimes. Finally, the paper concludes with a few open problems.
generated_abstract: Reed–Muller (RM) codes have long been conjectured to achieve Shannon capacity, yet their relationship with polar codes and the design of practical decoders remain incompletely understood. Both code families arise from the same Kronecker-power generator matrix, but they select its rows according to different principles: polarization uses conditional mutual information, whereas RM codes use row weights. We study this connection together with the highly symmetric structure of RM codes. Our approach exploits polarization in the RM ordering and the resulting concentration of synthesized channels, while also considering decoding procedures based on minimum-weight parity checks and recursive projection, decoding, and aggregation. These perspectives clarify why RM codes can have strong finite-length performance and why their symmetry is useful for low-complexity decoding. The analysis shows that an ordering closely related to RM ordering polarizes, yielding a capacity-achieving code on symmetric channels and providing a necessary condition for RM capacity achievement. Numerical results reported for short codes further show near-maximum-likelihood performance under several practical decoders, although equality between the resulting capacity-achieving code and the RM code itself is not established in general.

original_abstract: To ensure pedestrian friendly streets in the era of automated vehicles, reassessment of current policies, practices, design, rules and regulations of urban areas is of importance. This study investigates pedestrian crossing behaviour, as an important element of urban dynamics that is expected to be affected by the presence of automated vehicles. For this purpose, an interpretable machine learning framework is proposed to explore factors affecting pedestrians' wait time before crossing mid-block crosswalks in the presence of automated vehicles. To collect rich behavioural data, we developed a dynamic and immersive virtual reality experiment, with 180 participants from a heterogeneous population in 4 different locations in the Greater Toronto Area (GTA). Pedestrian wait time behaviour is then analyzed using a data-driven Cox Proportional Hazards (CPH) model, in which the linear combination of the covariates is replaced by a flexible non-linear deep neural network. The proposed model achieved a 5% improvement in goodness of fit, but more importantly, enabled us to incorporate a richer set of covariates. A game theoretic based interpretability method is used to understand the contribution of different covariates to the time pedestrians wait before crossing. Results show that the presence of automated vehicles on roads, wider lane widths, high density on roads, limited sight distance, and lack of walking habits are the main contributing factors to longer wait times. Our study suggested that, to move towards pedestrian-friendly urban areas, national level educational programs for children, enhanced safety measures for seniors, promotion of active modes of transportation, and revised traffic rules and regulations should be considered.
generated_abstract:
Understanding when and why pedestrians cross remains essential for safe urban mobility, particularly as automated vehicles enter mixed traffic. Crossing decisions depend on vehicle motion, time to collision, available gaps, signals, crosswalk configuration, pedestrian gaze, and communication between road users. Existing studies have examined these factors through naturalistic observation, gap-acceptance analysis, immersive virtual reality, and experiments with external human-machine interfaces, but reliable prediction and behavioral interpretation remain challenging.

We develop a data-driven framework for pedestrian crossing behavior that captures nonlinear relationships while retaining behaviorally meaningful information. The framework combines deep neural-network modeling with feature selection and numerical analysis of predicted probabilities and derivatives, enabling examination of how traffic, environmental, and communication variables influence crossing intention and waiting behavior. Immersive scenarios provide a controlled means of representing interactions with conventional and automated vehicles.

The results indicate that flexible nonlinear models can improve behavioral prediction and reveal the distinct roles of vehicle yielding, vehicle size and speed, pedestrian–vehicle timing, signals, and communicative cues. However, disaggregate outputs may be irregular and sensitive to estimation choices. Aggregation, regularization, and model ensembling produce more stable interpretations, supporting safer crossing-facility and automated-vehicle design.

original_abstract: Training neural networks is traditionally done by providing a sequence of random mini-batches sampled uniformly from the entire training data. In this work, we analyze the effect of curriculum learning, which involves the non-uniform sampling of mini-batches, on the training of deep networks, and specifically CNNs trained for image recognition. To employ curriculum learning, the training algorithm must resolve 2 problems: (i) sort the training examples by difficulty; (ii) compute a series of mini-batches that exhibit an increasing level of difficulty. We address challenge (i) using two methods: transfer learning from some competitive ``teacher" network, and bootstrapping. In our empirical evaluation, both methods show similar benefits in terms of increased learning speed and improved final performance on test data. We address challenge (ii) by investigating different pacing functions to guide the sampling. The empirical investigation includes a variety of network architectures, using images from CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and subsets of ImageNet. We conclude with a novel theoretical analysis of curriculum learning, where we show how it effectively modifies the optimization landscape. We then define the concept of an ideal curriculum, and show that under mild conditions it does not change the corresponding global minimum of the optimization function.
generated_abstract: Training deep neural networks remains costly and sensitive to the order and quality of the examples presented to the learner. Fixed curricula, manually designed schedules, and reward shaping require substantial prior knowledge, while noisy or difficult data can lead to inefficient optimization and overfitting. We formulate curriculum construction as an adaptive teaching problem in which a teacher observes the student’s learning behavior and selects training examples or tasks to maximize subsequent progress. The approach builds on curriculum learning, automated syllabus generation, reverse progression from goal states, transfer-based ordering, and data-driven sample weighting, while adopting the teacher–student interaction and reinforcement-learning perspective of learning to teach. It is applicable to recurrent, convolutional, and residual networks and to sequence, vision, and goal-oriented learning problems. By adapting the syllabus to the current competence of the student rather than following a fixed difficulty schedule, the framework seeks to accelerate convergence, reduce the amount of training data and computation required, and improve generalization when supervision is corrupted or tasks are challenging. The cited evidence establishes the promise of these principles, but does not determine a more specific implementation or empirical conclusion for this paper.

original_abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks fostered a newfound interest in generative models, resulting in a swelling wave of new works that new-coming researchers may find formidable to surf. In this paper, we intend to help those researchers, by splitting that incoming wave into six "fronts": Architectural Contributions, Conditional Techniques, Normalization and Constraint Contributions, Loss Functions, Image-to-image Translations, and Validation Metrics. The division in fronts organizes literature into approachable blocks, ultimately communicating to the reader how the area is evolving. Previous surveys in the area, which this works also tabulates, focus on a few of those fronts, leaving a gap that we propose to fill with a more integrated, comprehensive overview. Here, instead of an exhaustive survey, we opt for a straightforward review: our target is to be an entry point to this vast literature, and also to be able to update experienced researchers to the newest techniques.
generated_abstract: Generative adversarial networks have become a powerful framework for learning to synthesize realistic data, yet their practical use remains limited by unstable training, mode collapse, insufficient sample diversity, and the difficulty of producing high-quality images at scale. We study these challenges through the development of adversarial objectives, generator and discriminator architectures, progressive and multi-scale training strategies, conditional synthesis, and mechanisms for controlling latent variation. Building on advances in semi-supervised learning, coarse-to-fine generation, high-resolution image synthesis, and style-based representation, we organize the principal design choices according to the quality, diversity, stability, controllability, and resolution they affect. We further consider how visual Turing tests, inception-based measures, distributional distances, and dedicated measures of interpolation and disentanglement can be used to evaluate generated samples. Our analysis shows that no single architectural or loss modification resolves all shortcomings: improvements in fidelity may reduce variation, while greater diversity can complicate optimization. The results motivate combining complementary architectural, regularization, and training techniques, and indicate that scalable evaluation and more controllable representations remain central directions for future GAN research.

original_abstract: Local differential privacy (LDP) can provide each user with strong privacy guarantees under untrusted data curators while ensuring accurate statistics derived from privatized data. Due to its powerfulness, LDP has been widely adopted to protect privacy in various tasks (e.g., heavy hitters discovery, probability estimation) and systems (e.g., Google Chrome, Apple iOS). Although ${\epsilon}$-LDP has been proposed for many years, the more general notion of $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP has only been studied in very few papers, which mainly consider mean estimation for numeric data. Besides, prior solutions achieve $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP by leveraging Gaussian mechanism, which leads to low accuracy of the aggregated results. In this paper, we propose novel mechanisms that achieve $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP with high utility in data analytics and machine learning. Specifically, we first design $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP algorithms for collecting multi-dimensional numeric data, which can ensure higher accuracy than the optimal Gaussian mechanism while guaranteeing strong privacy for each user. Then, we investigate different local protocols for categorical attributes under $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP. Furthermore, we conduct theoretical analysis on the error bound and variance of the proposed algorithms. Experimental results on real and synthetic datasets demonstrate the high data utility of our proposed algorithms on both simple data statistics and complex machine learning models.
generated_abstract: Local differential privacy enables statistical analysis while keeping each user’s data private from the data collector, but local randomization can substantially reduce utility, particularly for multidimensional, unbounded, and structured data. We study this privacy–utility tradeoff across data collection, estimation, and machine learning. Building on mechanisms for categorical, numerical, set-valued, key-value, and marginal data, we examine how locally randomized reports support frequency and mean estimation, Gaussian mean estimation, regression, classification, stochastic gradient descent, and neural-network training. We also relate practical constructions to information-theoretic lower bounds and minimax procedures, and to sharper analyses of Gaussian, Exponential, randomized-response, and staircase mechanisms. Our treatment emphasizes both the design of client-side perturbation and the calibration and post-processing performed by the aggregator. The resulting evidence shows that local privacy is compatible with useful inference, but accuracy depends critically on the domain, dimensionality, privacy budget, and interaction allowed by the protocol. No single mechanism is uniformly optimal: carefully tailored mechanisms and iterative or task-specific estimation procedures can markedly improve utility over generic perturbation, while fundamental accuracy limits remain for unbounded and high-dimensional problems.

original_abstract: We investigate the combination of actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithms with uniform large-scale experience replay and propose solutions for two challenges: (a) efficient actor-critic learning with experience replay (b) stability of very off-policy learning. We employ those insights to accelerate hyper-parameter sweeps in which all participating agents run concurrently and share their experience via a common replay module. To this end we analyze the bias-variance tradeoffs in V-trace, a form of importance sampling for actor-critic methods. Based on our analysis, we then argue for mixing experience sampled from replay with on-policy experience, and propose a new trust region scheme that scales effectively to data distributions where V-trace becomes unstable. We provide extensive empirical validation of the proposed solution. We further show the benefits of this setup by demonstrating state-of-the-art data efficiency on Atari among agents trained up until 200M environment frames.
generated_abstract: Deep reinforcement learning has demonstrated strong performance in visual control, yet its practical application remains limited by high sample complexity, unstable off-policy learning, and the computational cost of training. We address these difficulties by building on deep Q-learning and actor-critic methods, experience replay, prioritized sampling, multi-step return estimation, and distributed actor–learner architectures. Our approach combines parallel data collection with replay-based learning and off-policy correction, while using policy-evaluation and optimization mechanisms designed to control the bias–variance trade-off. It further accommodates stochastic policies and adaptive return choices, drawing on trust-region and maximum-entropy principles where appropriate. This design targets both efficient reuse of experience and stable improvement when behavior and target policies differ substantially. Across challenging Atari and continuous-control settings, the resulting agent demonstrates that throughput, sample efficiency, and robustness need not be treated as mutually exclusive objectives. The results also indicate that improvements such as prioritized replay, asynchronous or decoupled learning, reliable multi-step updates, and carefully constrained policy optimization are complementary, although their benefits depend on the interaction between architecture, data distribution, and task characteristics.

original_abstract: The design of deep graph models still remains to be investigated and the crucial part is how to explore and exploit the knowledge from different hops of neighbors in an efficient way. In this paper, we propose a novel RNN-like deep graph neural network architecture by incorporating AdaBoost into the computation of network; and the proposed graph convolutional network called AdaGCN~(AdaBoosting Graph Convolutional Network) has the ability to efficiently extract knowledge from high-order neighbors and integrate knowledge from different hops of neighbors into the network in an AdaBoost way. We also present the architectural difference between AdaGCN and existing graph convolutional methods to show the benefits of our proposal. Finally, extensive experiments demonstrate the state-of-the-art prediction performance and the computational advantage of our approach AdaGCN.
generated_abstract: Graph-structured data require models that combine node attributes with topology, yet standard graph convolutional networks often rely on shallow, repeated neighborhood aggregation. Increasing depth enlarges the receptive field but can cause over-smoothing, entangle propagation with feature transformation, and limit the ability to distinguish graph structures or represent diverse neighborhood-mixing relationships. We study these limitations and develop a graph neural architecture that preserves information from multiple neighborhood ranges while allowing node representations to adapt to the relevant scale. The approach builds on localized spectral graph convolutions and their efficient first-order approximations, interprets propagation as Laplacian smoothing, and incorporates insights from attention, higher-order neighborhood mixing, simplified propagation, and jumping representations. By separating the use of graph structure from feature transformation and combining information across depths, the resulting model can exploit larger receptive fields without relying solely on repeated low-pass filtering. Experiments on semi-supervised node and graph representation-learning tasks show that multi-scale, deeper propagation improves performance over conventional graph convolutional networks and remains effective when labeled data are limited. Our analysis clarifies both the benefits and fundamental limits of depth in graph neural networks.

original_abstract: This paper seeks to answer a simple but fundamental question: what role can non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) play in massive multi-in multi-out (MIMO)? It is well established that power-domain NOMA schemes can outperform conventional orthogonal multiple access schemes in cellular networks. However, this fact does not imply that NOMA is the most efficient way to communicate in massive MIMO setups, where the base stations have many more antennas than there are users in the cell. These setups are becoming the norm in future networks and are usually studied by assuming spatial multiplexing of the users using linear multi-user beamforming. To answer the above-mentioned question, we analyze and compare the performance achieved by NOMA and multi-user beamforming in both non-line-of-sight and line-of-sight scenarios. We reveal that the latter scheme gives the highest average sum rate in massive MIMO setups. We also identify specific cases where NOMA is the better choice in massive MIMO and explain how NOMA plays an essential role in creating a hybrid of NOMA and multi-user beamforming that is shown to perform better than two standalone schemes do.
generated_abstract: Massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) are promising technologies for meeting the throughput, connectivity, and efficiency requirements of future wireless networks. Their integration, however, introduces coupled challenges in channel acquisition, user ordering, beamforming, power allocation, and successive interference cancellation. In particular, the favorable propagation and channel-hardening properties that simplify massive-MIMO transmission may be weakened by spatial correlation, limited scattering, or other propagation conditions, making conventional ergodic-rate bounds and reliance on statistical channel information inaccurate. We investigate massive-MIMO-NOMA transmission in time-division duplex and frequency-division duplex settings, considering practical channel-state-information acquisition, including shared or limited pilots and feedback. The analysis builds on decomposing transmission into manageable NOMA channels, multiple-antenna user clustering and beamforming, and joint allocation of transmit power and feedback resources. Achievable-rate bounds and performance comparisons characterize the effects of channel hardening, interference suppression, CSI accuracy, and system dimensions. The results indicate that NOMA can improve spectral efficiency and user accommodation over orthogonal access when users, beams, and powers are appropriately coordinated, but multiuser beamforming may be preferable as the number of groups increases.

original_abstract: In [1, 2], we have explored the theoretical aspects of feature extraction optimization processes for solving largescale problems and overcoming machine learning limitations. Majority of optimization algorithms that have been introduced in [1, 2] guarantee the optimal performance of supervised learning, given offline and discrete data, to deal with curse of dimensionality (CoD) problem. These algorithms, however, are not tailored for solving emerging learning problems. One of the important issues caused by online data is lack of sufficient samples per class. Further, traditional machine learning algorithms cannot achieve accurate training based on limited distributed data, as data has proliferated and dispersed significantly. Machine learning employs a strict model or embedded engine to train and predict which still fails to learn unseen classes and sufficiently use online data. In this chapter, we introduce these challenges elaborately. We further investigate Meta-Learning (MTL) algorithm, and their application and promises to solve the emerging problems by answering how autonomous agents can learn to learn?.
generated_abstract: Few-shot learning seeks to recognize or solve new tasks from only a small number of labeled examples, where conventional supervised training readily overfits and cannot adapt rapidly. We study meta-learning as a means of acquiring experience across tasks and transferring that experience to unseen classes, regressions, or other learning problems. Building on metric-based approaches, Matching Networks, Relation Networks, and Prototypical Networks perform prediction by comparing query representations with support examples, while model-based approaches such as Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning and its stabilized variants learn parameters that can be rapidly fine-tuned. Other directions address the ambiguity of limited data through probabilistic model distributions, synthesize additional examples through hallucination, adapt deep networks through learned scaling and shifting, or seek generalization across heterogeneous task structures. Together, these developments establish episodic training, task diversity, and suitable inductive biases as central requirements for effective adaptation. They also expose persistent limitations, including sensitivity to architecture and optimization, high computational cost, task ambiguity, and restricted transfer across task structures. The resulting perspective identifies few-shot learning as a problem of balancing rapid adaptation with robust generalization, while the cited material does not determine a more specific proposed algorithm or empirical conclusion.

original_abstract: Edge computing is an emerging concept based on distributing computing, storage, and control services closer to end network nodes. Edge computing lies at the heart of the fifth generation (5G) wireless systems and beyond. While current state-of-the-art networks communicate, compute, and process data in a centralized manner (at the cloud), for latency and compute-centric applications, both radio access and computational resources must be brought closer to the edge, harnessing the availability of computing and storage-enabled small cell base stations in proximity to the end devices. Furthermore, the network infrastructure must enable a distributed edge decision-making service that learns to adapt to the network dynamics with minimal latency and optimize network deployment and operation accordingly. This article will provide a fresh look to the concept of edge computing by first discussing the applications that the network edge must provide, with a special emphasis on the ensuing challenges in enabling ultra-reliable and low-latency edge computing services for mission-critical applications such as virtual reality (VR), vehicle-to-everything (V2X), edge artificial intelligence (AI), and so forth. Furthermore, several case studies where the edge is key are explored followed by insights and prospect for future work.
generated_abstract: We study the design of mobile edge computing networks for intelligent and mission-critical applications, where resource-constrained devices must support stringent latency and reliability requirements over dynamic wireless links. Conventional designs based on average throughput, queue length, or delay are inadequate because rare queueing and communication events can violate ultra-reliable low-latency requirements. Building on edge learning and MEC architectures, we consider the coupled management of wireless and computational resources, including task offloading, local computation, transmit power, user–server association, and mobility. We formulate reliability through probabilistic queue-length constraints and account for channel dynamics, server workloads, and the spatial and temporal variation of user movement. A tractable design combines extreme value theory with Lyapunov stochastic optimization and matching-based association across different timescales; user-centric mobility management and energy-efficient power control are incorporated where dense deployments make centralized control impractical. The resulting framework exposes the power–delay–reliability tradeoff and supports distributed operation at the network edge. Numerical evaluations indicate that dynamic association and resource adaptation can provide lower delay, high-reliability task computation, and improved energy efficiency compared with fixed or average-based baselines.

original_abstract: Automatic Post-Editing (APE) aims to correct systematic errors in a machine translated text. This is primarily useful when the machine translation (MT) system is not accessible for improvement, leaving APE as a viable option to improve translation quality as a downstream task - which is the focus of this thesis. This field has received less attention compared to MT due to several reasons, which include: the limited availability of data to perform a sound research, contrasting views reported by different researchers about the effectiveness of APE, and limited attention from the industry to use APE in current production pipelines. In this thesis, we perform a thorough investigation of APE as a downstream task in order to: i) understand its potential to improve translation quality; ii) advance the core technology - starting from classical methods to recent deep-learning based solutions; iii) cope with limited and sparse data; iv) better leverage multiple input sources; v) mitigate the task-specific problem of over-correction; vi) enhance neural decoding to leverage external knowledge; and vii) establish an online learning framework to handle data diversity in real-time. All the above contributions are discussed across several chapters, and most of them are evaluated in the APE shared task organized each year at the Conference on Machine Translation. Our efforts in improving the technology resulted in the best system at the 2017 APE shared task, and our work on online learning received a distinguished paper award at the Italian Conference on Computational Linguistics. Overall, outcomes and findings of our work have boost interest among researchers and attracted industries to examine this technology to solve real-word problems.
generated_abstract: Automatic post-editing (APE) aims to improve machine-translation output without modifying the underlying translation system, thereby reducing human post-editing effort. The task is challenging because the post-editor must preserve correct content while making only the edits required by the source sentence and the raw translation, often in a low-resource setting. Building on encoder–decoder neural translation, attention-based alignment, and multi-source modeling, we formulate APE as a neural sequence-to-sequence problem that jointly exploits the source sentence and its machine-translated hypothesis. We examine complementary strategies for improving robustness, including synthetic training data, ensembles or log-linear combinations of specialized models, explicit preference for retaining unchanged words, and quality-estimation signals for selecting among candidate post-edits. The resulting framework is designed to limit overcorrection and to remain faithful to the original translation while correcting its errors. Experiments on benchmark APE tasks show consistent improvements over uncorrected machine translation and established phrase-based and neural post-editing baselines, with larger gains when the initial translation is of lower quality. The results also demonstrate that post-editing and quality estimation can reinforce one another.

original_abstract: We consider a variant of the classic Ski Rental online algorithm with applications to machine learning. In our variant, we allow the skier access to a black-box machine-learning algorithm that provides an estimate of the probability that there will be at most a threshold number of ski-days. We derive a class of optimal randomized algorithms to determine the strategy that minimizes the worst-case expected competitive ratio for the skier given a prediction from the machine learning algorithm,and analyze the performance and robustness of these algorithms.
generated_abstract: We study how machine-learned predictions can improve online decision-making under uncertainty while retaining guarantees when predictions are inaccurate. Classical online algorithms hedge against arbitrary future inputs and are evaluated against an offline optimum, whereas prediction-based methods can exploit regularities in observed data but may fail when predictions are poor. This tension arises in problems including caching, ski rental, and non-clairvoyant job scheduling, and also appears in advertising auctions, where reserve-price optimization is difficult because opportunity types are heterogeneous and the objective is non-convex. We build on approaches that treat predictions as black-box advice, relate performance to prediction loss, and reduce learning objectives to standard statistical prediction problems. Our perspective combines the benefits of these approaches: algorithms should improve as prediction error decreases, yet remain robust under unreliable advice and retain worst-case safeguards. We also consider average-case analysis, which can yield strategies distinct from worst-case competitive ones. The resulting framework clarifies how predictive accuracy, distributional assumptions, and competitive guarantees interact, and demonstrates that learning can enhance online algorithms without requiring trust in the predictor or its internal construction.

original_abstract: While deep learning (DL)-based networked systems have shown great potential in various applications, a key drawback is that Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in DL are blackboxes and nontransparent for network operators. The lack of interpretability makes DL-based networked systems challenging to operate and troubleshoot, which further prevents DL-based networked systems from deploying in practice. In this paper, we propose TranSys, a novel framework to explain DL-based networked systems for practical deployment. Transys categorizes current DL-based networked systems and introduces different explanation methods based on decision tree and hypergraph to effectively explain DL-based networked systems. TranSys can explain the DNN policies in the form of decision trees and highlight critical components based on analysis over hypergraph. We evaluate TranSys over several typical DL-based networked systems and demonstrate that Transys can provide human-readable explanations for network operators. We also present three use cases of Transys, which could (i) help network operators troubleshoot DL-based networked systems, (ii) improve the decision latency and resource consumption of DL-based networked systems by ~10x on different metrics, and (iii) provide suggestions on daily operations for network operators when incidences occur.
generated_abstract: We study the growing use of deep learning and reinforcement learning in computer-networking systems, where high predictive or operational performance is accompanied by limited insight into how decisions are made. This lack of transparency complicates debugging, diagnosing anomalous behavior, assessing generalization, and establishing correctness and security. Building on work in interpretable machine learning, feature-attribution methods, representation analysis, graph-based explanation, and formal verification, we examine how these perspectives can be applied to network models for routing, traffic management, packet classification, video adaptation, and related optimization tasks. We distinguish explanations of individual predictions from analyses of learned representations and from guarantees about behavior over specified inputs. We further relate learned models to their structured networking inputs, including topology, traffic, rules, and routing decisions, and discuss the limitations of post hoc explanations when explanations are incomplete or unstable. The resulting perspective shows that interpretability can reveal semantically meaningful internal structure and undesirable decisions, while verification can establish stronger behavioral properties. We conclude that trustworthy learning-based networking requires combining predictive evaluation with explanation, systematic testing, and formal verification, rather than relying on accuracy alone.

original_abstract: This paper proposes the first model-free Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework to synthesise policies for unknown, and continuous-state Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), such that a given linear temporal property is satisfied. We convert the given property into a Limit Deterministic Buchi Automaton (LDBA), namely a finite-state machine expressing the property. Exploiting the structure of the LDBA, we shape a synchronous reward function on-the-fly, so that an RL algorithm can synthesise a policy resulting in traces that probabilistically satisfy the linear temporal property. This probability (certificate) is also calculated in parallel with policy learning when the state space of the MDP is finite: as such, the RL algorithm produces a policy that is certified with respect to the property. Under the assumption of finite state space, theoretical guarantees are provided on the convergence of the RL algorithm to an optimal policy, maximising the above probability. We also show that our method produces ''best available'' control policies when the logical property cannot be satisfied. In the general case of a continuous state space, we propose a neural network architecture for RL and we empirically show that the algorithm finds satisfying policies, if there exist such policies. The performance of the proposed framework is evaluated via a set of numerical examples and benchmarks, where we observe an improvement of one order of magnitude in the number of iterations required for the policy synthesis, compared to existing approaches whenever available.
generated_abstract: We address the synthesis of control policies for reinforcement learning in unknown, stochastic environments subject to temporal-logic requirements. Standard reinforcement learning can optimize an unknown performance criterion, but it does not by itself ensure safety or liveness, while model-based approaches require transition information that may be unavailable or inaccurate. We formulate the interaction between the controller and its environment as a Markov decision process and represent the specification by a temporal-logic automaton. Building on constrained exploration, permissive safe strategies, and model-free learning, we construct a synchronized product and use specification-dependent rewards to guide policy synthesis toward behaviors satisfying the required property. The resulting approach avoids exhaustive construction of the original model and can operate when transition probabilities, and in some settings the graph structure, are initially unknown. We establish probabilistic satisfaction guarantees under the stated assumptions and characterize the relationship between the learned objective and the probability of satisfying the temporal specification. The approach also preserves safe behavior during exploration, although optimality can be limited beyond the supported specification fragment. Numerical motion-planning examples demonstrate its effectiveness and reduced computational requirements.

original_abstract: Many inferential and learning tasks can be accomplished efficiently by means of distributed optimization algorithms where the network topology plays a critical role in driving the local interactions among neighboring agents. There is a large body of literature examining the effect of the graph structure on the performance of optimization strategies. In this article, we examine the inverse problem and consider the reverse question: How much information does observing the behavior at the nodes convey about the underlying network structure used for optimization? Over large-scale networks, the difficulty of addressing such inverse questions (or problems) is compounded by the fact that usually only a limited portion of nodes can be probed, giving rise to a second important question: Despite the presence of several unobserved nodes, are partial and local observations still sufficient to discover the graph linking the probed nodes? The article surveys recent advances on this inverse learning problem and related questions. Examples of applications are provided to illustrate how the interplay between graph learning and distributed optimization arises in practice, e.g., in cognitive engineered systems such as distributed detection, or in other real-world problems such as the mechanism of opinion formation over social networks and the mechanism of coordination in biological networks. A unifying framework for examining the reconstruction error will be described, which allows to devise and examine various estimation strategies enabling successful graph learning. The relevance of specific network attributes, such as sparsity versus density of connections, and node degree concentration, is discussed in relation to the topology inference goal. It is shown how universal (i.e., data-driven) clustering algorithms can be exploited to solve the graph learning problem.
generated_abstract: Inferring the interaction topology of a large adaptive diffusion network from observations of only a fraction of its agents is challenging: the observer sees algorithm outputs rather than raw data, and the total network size may be unknown. Existing tomography results establish recoverability in low-observability settings under stochastic assumptions on the latent network, while graph-learning results indicate that degree concentration, rather than sparsity, can provide the separation needed for identification. We study this problem in the dense latent regime, where connectivity is not sparse and only the observable subnetwork is to be reconstructed. We analyze the Granger estimator of the combination matrix and show that, under suitable stability and symmetry conditions, it exhibits an identifiability gap between interacting and non-interacting observable pairs as the network grows. Consequently, a universal clustering procedure can consistently distinguish these two classes and recover the local interaction profile with high probability. The result demonstrates that consistent tomography remains possible despite dense hidden connectivity and severe partial observation, and that concentration of node degrees—not sparsity—is the fundamental mechanism enabling local graph recovery. Numerical experiments illustrate the predicted behavior for finite networks.

original_abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has recently led to many breakthroughs on a range of complex control tasks. However, the agent's decision-making process is generally not transparent. The lack of interpretability hinders the applicability of RL in safety-critical scenarios. While several methods have attempted to interpret vision-based RL, most come without detailed explanation for the agent's behaviour. In this paper, we propose a self-supervised interpretable framework, which can discover causal features to enable easy interpretation of RL agents even for non-experts. Specifically, a self-supervised interpretable network (SSINet) is employed to produce fine-grained attention masks for highlighting task-relevant information, which constitutes most evidence for the agent's decisions. We verify and evaluate our method on several Atari 2600 games as well as Duckietown, which is a challenging self-driving car simulator environment. The results show that our method renders causal explanations and empirical evidences about how the agent makes decisions and why the agent performs well or badly, especially when transferred to novel scenes. Overall, our method provides valuable insight into the internal decision-making process of vision-based RL. In addition, our method does not use any external labelled data, and thus demonstrates the possibility to learn high-quality mask through a self-supervised manner, which may shed light on new paradigms for label-free vision learning such as self-supervised segmentation and detection.
generated_abstract: Deep reinforcement learning agents can achieve strong performance from visual observations, yet their policies remain difficult to understand, diagnose, and trust. We address this gap in Atari 2600 environments by studying how attention and saliency can expose the information used for action selection and how such mechanisms affect learning. Building on attention-augmented Q-learning, recurrent and self-attentive agents, interpretable Q-network architectures, and post-hoc visualisation through saliency and meaningful perturbation, we consider attention as both an explanatory bottleneck and a source of improved state representations. Our approach incorporates trainable attention into a deep Q-learning agent, producing visualisations of task-relevant regions while retaining the ability to learn effective policies without additional supervision. The resulting explanations make it possible to inspect what agents attend to, distinguish appropriate from inappropriate decision cues, and follow changes in behaviour during training. Experiments in the Arcade Learning Environment show that attention can yield competitive, and in some settings improved, performance while providing interpretable policy information. The results further indicate that useful policies may employ multiple foci and vary attention over time, particularly when observations are partially observable.

original_abstract: Concolic testing is a test generation technique which works effectively by integrating random testing generation and symbolic execution. Existing concolic testing engines focus on numeric programs. Heap-manipulating programs make extensive use of complex heap objects like trees and lists. Testing such programs is challenging due to multiple reasons. Firstly, test inputs for such program are required to satisfy non-trivial constraints which must be specified precisely. Secondly, precisely encoding and solving path conditions in such programs are challenging and often expensive. In this work, we propose the first concolic testing engine called CSF for heap-manipulating programs based on separation logic. CSF effectively combines specification-based testing and concolic execution for test input generation. It is evaluated on a set of challenging heap-manipulating programs. The results show that CSF generates valid test inputs with high coverage efficiently. Furthermore, we show that CSF can be potentially used in combination with precondition inference tools to reduce the user effort.
generated_abstract: Automatic test generation for programs that manipulate complex heap structures remains difficult. Search-based testing can discover sequences of method calls that construct inputs through legal interfaces, but it struggles to reach program elements whose execution depends on structural properties of those inputs. Symbolic execution can describe such dependencies and generate path conditions, yet it does not by itself determine the method-call sequences needed to instantiate valid structures. We propose a combined approach in which symbolic execution characterises the relationship between execution paths and input structures, while search-based techniques solve the resulting optimisation problems to construct test cases. The approach is informed by separation-logic descriptions of heap preconditions and by symbolic techniques for context-sensitive initialization, thereby reducing invalid or incomplete inputs. It also reflects the complementary use of inexpensive exploration and selective concolic execution to address difficult path conditions without incurring unrestricted path explosion. The resulting framework targets shape, size, and value properties of heap data structures and supports their use in test generation. Preliminary evaluation indicates that it can produce legal, structurally complex inputs and exercise relevant program behaviour, suggesting a practical direction for automated testing of heap-manipulating programs.

original_abstract: Prior work on controllable text generation usually assumes that the controlled attribute can take on one of a small set of values known a priori. In this work, we propose a novel task, where the syntax of a generated sentence is controlled rather by a sentential exemplar. To evaluate quantitatively with standard metrics, we create a novel dataset with human annotations. We also develop a variational model with a neural module specifically designed for capturing syntactic knowledge and several multitask training objectives to promote disentangled representation learning. Empirically, the proposed model is observed to achieve improvements over baselines and learn to capture desirable characteristics.
generated_abstract: We address the difficulty of generating natural-language text that is fluent, diverse, coherent, and controllable. Conventional recurrent language models generate locally, making global properties such as style, topic, syntax, and discourse structure difficult to represent and manipulate. We build on sentence-level variational representations, hierarchical latent variables, and disentangled factors for syntax, semantics, style, and conversational intent. We further consider generation by editing prototype sentences, retrieving exemplars as soft templates, and learning discrete templates, thereby combining global planning with faithful and interpretable realization. These approaches impose semantic structure through auxiliary objectives, attribute constraints, paraphrastic or word-order information, and bag-of-words signals, while addressing the optimization difficulties and posterior collapse that arise in latent-variable text models. Across language modeling, dialogue, paraphrasing, style transfer, summarization, and data-to-text generation, structured representations and exemplar-informed decoding improve the quality, diversity, interpretability, and controllability of generated text. The results indicate that effective text generation benefits from modeling content and realization separately and from providing generation with explicit global guidance rather than relying solely on unrestricted left-to-right decoding.

original_abstract: Hyperspectral images (HSI) provide rich spectral information that contributed to the successful performance improvement of numerous computer vision tasks. However, it can only be achieved at the expense of images' spatial resolution. Hyperspectral image super-resolution (HSI-SR) addresses this problem by fusing low resolution (LR) HSI with multispectral image (MSI) carrying much higher spatial resolution (HR). All existing HSI-SR approaches require the LR HSI and HR MSI to be well registered and the reconstruction accuracy of the HR HSI relies heavily on the registration accuracy of different modalities. This paper exploits the uncharted problem domain of HSI-SR without the requirement of multi-modality registration. Given the unregistered LR HSI and HR MSI with overlapped regions, we design a unique unsupervised learning structure linking the two unregistered modalities by projecting them into the same statistical space through the same encoder. The mutual information (MI) is further adopted to capture the non-linear statistical dependencies between the representations from two modalities (carrying spatial information) and their raw inputs. By maximizing the MI, spatial correlations between different modalities can be well characterized to further reduce the spectral distortion. A collaborative $l_{2,1}$ norm is employed as the reconstruction error instead of the more common $l_2$ norm, so that individual pixels can be recovered as accurately as possible. With this design, the network allows to extract correlated spectral and spatial information from unregistered images that better preserves the spectral information. The proposed method is referred to as unregistered and unsupervised mutual Dirichlet Net ($u^2$-MDN). Extensive experimental results using benchmark HSI datasets demonstrate the superior performance of $u^2$-MDN as compared to the state-of-the-art.
generated_abstract: Hyperspectral imaging provides rich spectral information but is commonly limited by poor spatial resolution. We address hyperspectral image super-resolution, namely the reconstruction of a high-resolution hyperspectral image from a low-resolution hyperspectral image and a spatially detailed multispectral or RGB observation, while avoiding spectral distortion. The approach is motivated by observation models, low-rank and tensor structure, spectral unmixing, and physical camera responses, together with the capacity of convolutional networks to learn nonlinear image priors. In particular, it builds on end-to-end deep convolutional mappings, residual learning, three-dimensional spatial–spectral processing, and model-based network unfolding. Because high-resolution hyperspectral ground truth and accurate point-spread and spectral-response functions are often unavailable, an unsupervised or jointly optimized formulation is required; shared representations, coupled encoders and decoders, adaptive response estimation, and spectral consistency provide suitable mechanisms. The cited material therefore determines a fusion framework that combines learned spatial enhancement with explicit preservation of spectral fidelity and data-generation constraints. It does not determine the specific architecture, objective, training procedure, or quantitative conclusions of the present study.

original_abstract: This paper presents SimCLR: a simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations. We simplify recently proposed contrastive self-supervised learning algorithms without requiring specialized architectures or a memory bank. In order to understand what enables the contrastive prediction tasks to learn useful representations, we systematically study the major components of our framework. We show that (1) composition of data augmentations plays a critical role in defining effective predictive tasks, (2) introducing a learnable nonlinear transformation between the representation and the contrastive loss substantially improves the quality of the learned representations, and (3) contrastive learning benefits from larger batch sizes and more training steps compared to supervised learning. By combining these findings, we are able to considerably outperform previous methods for self-supervised and semi-supervised learning on ImageNet. A linear classifier trained on self-supervised representations learned by SimCLR achieves 76.5% top-1 accuracy, which is a 7% relative improvement over previous state-of-the-art, matching the performance of a supervised ResNet-50. When fine-tuned on only 1% of the labels, we achieve 85.8% top-5 accuracy, outperforming AlexNet with 100X fewer labels.
generated_abstract: Learning visual representations without human annotation remains a central challenge in computer vision, since conventional convolutional networks require large labeled datasets and do not scale readily to new domains. We investigate self-supervised learning as a means of extracting transferable semantic features from unlabeled images. Our approach builds on pretext objectives that require recognizing image rotations, predicting spatial context, arranging jigsaw tiles, and discriminating transformed instances, as well as on contrastive and mutual-information objectives that bring representations of related views together while separating unrelated samples. We further consider mechanisms that improve the consistency and scale of contrastive learning, including non-parametric dictionaries, queues, and moving-averaged encoders, together with careful choices of network architecture and training procedure. The resulting representations are evaluated through linear classification, fine-tuning, object detection, segmentation, and recognition with limited labels. Across these settings, self-supervised features capture semantically meaningful content and transfer substantially better than randomly initialized features, in some cases matching or surpassing supervised pre-training. These findings show that unlabeled visual data can provide an effective supervisory signal and substantially narrow the gap between unsupervised and supervised representation learning.

original_abstract: Existing analysis work in machine reading comprehension (MRC) is largely concerned with evaluating the capabilities of systems. However, the capabilities of datasets are not assessed for benchmarking language understanding precisely. We propose a semi-automated, ablation-based methodology for this challenge; By checking whether questions can be solved even after removing features associated with a skill requisite for language understanding, we evaluate to what degree the questions do not require the skill. Experiments on 10 datasets (e.g., CoQA, SQuAD v2.0, and RACE) with a strong baseline model show that, for example, the relative scores of a baseline model provided with content words only and with shuffled sentence words in the context are on average 89.2% and 78.5% of the original score, respectively. These results suggest that most of the questions already answered correctly by the model do not necessarily require grammatical and complex reasoning. For precise benchmarking, MRC datasets will need to take extra care in their design to ensure that questions can correctly evaluate the intended skills.
generated_abstract: Machine reading comprehension seeks to answer questions from natural-language passages, yet progress measured on existing benchmarks may not reflect robust language understanding. Systems can exploit lexical overlap, question- or passage-specific cues, and answerability shortcuts, while still failing on adversarial distractions, paraphrases, coreference, pragmatic interpretation, and reasoning across multiple sentences. We examine how benchmark design and evaluation shape these conclusions. Building on extractive question answering over SQuAD, conversational answering in CoQA, paraphrased understanding in DuoRC, grade-school reasoning in ARC, and challenge sets for adversarial and multi-sentence inference, we organize the principal task settings, required reasoning skills, and sources of difficulty. We further consider unanswerable questions, readability, and diagnostic baselines that reveal when passages or questions can be ignored. This perspective shows that high performance on conventional extractive benchmarks does not establish general comprehension: substantial gaps remain between machine and human performance when answers require inference, external knowledge, discourse tracking, or abstention. Reliable progress therefore depends on complementary datasets and evaluations that suppress superficial cues and directly test the reasoning abilities required for understanding.

original_abstract: Spatio-temporal action localization is a challenging yet fascinating task that aims to detect and classify human actions in video clips. In this paper, we develop a high-level video understanding module which can encode interactions between actors and objects both in space and time. In our formulation, spatio-temporal relationships are learned by performing self-attention operations on a graph structure connecting entities from consecutive clips. Noticeably, the use of graph learning is unprecedented for this task. From a computational point of view, the proposed module is backbone independent by design and does not need end-to-end training. When tested on the AVA dataset, it demonstrates a 10-16% relative mAP improvement over the baseline. Further, it can outperform or bring performances comparable to state-of-the-art models which require heavy end-to-end and synchronized training on multiple GPUs. Code is publicly available at: this https URL.
generated_abstract: We address the problem of learning effective spatiotemporal representations for recognizing and detecting human actions in videos. Appearance in individual frames and motion across frames provide complementary evidence, yet conventional 2D convolutional networks often treat them independently, while unconstrained 3D networks are computationally demanding and may not exploit their relationship efficiently. Building on two-stream architectures with dense optical flow, 3D convolutional networks, residual learning, factorized spatial and temporal filters, long-term temporal convolutions, and collaborative feature learning, we develop an end-to-end convolutional approach that jointly captures spatial appearance, temporal motion, and action structure over an extended temporal context. The design enables information exchange between spatial and motion pathways, progressively enlarges the spatiotemporal receptive field, and supports localization by linking temporally consistent action predictions into tubes. We evaluate the resulting representation on standard action-recognition and action-detection benchmarks, comparing alternative temporal extents, fusion strategies, and spatiotemporal operations. The experiments demonstrate that explicitly modeling appearance–motion interactions and longer-range temporal dependencies improves recognition and localization over frame-based or independently learned representations, while retaining the practical advantages of convolutional architectures.

original_abstract: Low bit-width integer weights and activations are very important for efficient inference, especially with respect to lower power consumption. We propose Monte Carlo methods to quantize the weights and activations of pre-trained neural networks without any re-training. By performing importance sampling we obtain quantized low bit-width integer values from full-precision weights and activations. The precision, sparsity, and complexity are easily configurable by the amount of sampling performed. Our approach, called Monte Carlo Quantization (MCQ), is linear in both time and space, with the resulting quantized, sparse networks showing minimal accuracy loss when compared to the original full-precision networks. Our method either outperforms or achieves competitive results on multiple benchmarks compared to previous quantization methods that do require additional training.
generated_abstract: Deep neural networks deliver high predictive accuracy but demand substantial computation, memory, and energy, limiting their deployment on low-power and embedded hardware and making training costly. We address this problem by investigating low-precision representations throughout neural-network computation. Building on binary and ternary weight schemes, stochastic discretization, learned quantizers, and integer-based training, we consider the coordinated reduction of precision in weights, activations, gradients, and error signals. The resulting direction replaces general floating-point multiplications with sign changes, shifts, additions, and bit operations, while retaining sufficient numerical flexibility for optimization. In particular, training must account for the mismatch between discrete forward and backward computations and the continuous parameters used to accumulate updates; scaling factors, thresholds, and trainable quantization rules provide mechanisms for controlling this mismatch. Experiments on standard vision benchmarks, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, SVHN, and ImageNet, establish that substantial compression and computational savings are possible with limited accuracy degradation, and in some settings improved accuracy. These results support low-bitwidth training and inference as practical approaches for efficient hardware implementations.

original_abstract: The advent of deep learning has given rise to neural scene representations - learned mathematical models of a 3D environment. However, many of these representations do not explicitly reason about geometry and thus do not account for the underlying 3D structure of the scene. In contrast, geometric deep learning has explored 3D-structure-aware representations of scene geometry, but requires explicit 3D supervision. We propose Scene Representation Networks (SRNs), a continuous, 3D-structure-aware scene representation that encodes both geometry and appearance. SRNs represent scenes as continuous functions that map world coordinates to a feature representation of local scene properties. By formulating the image formation as a differentiable ray-marching algorithm, SRNs can be trained end-to-end from only 2D observations, without access to depth or geometry. This formulation naturally generalizes across scenes, learning powerful geometry and appearance priors in the process. We demonstrate the potential of SRNs by evaluating them for novel view synthesis, few-shot reconstruction, joint shape and appearance interpolation, and unsupervised discovery of a non-rigid face model.
generated_abstract: Recovering three-dimensional structure from one or more two-dimensional images remains challenging because the observation is incomplete, viewpoint-dependent, and often lacks explicit geometric supervision. Existing learning-based approaches address this problem by transferring shape priors from synthetic models, recurrently aggregating multiple views, or learning representations from unlabelled images through differentiable projection and rendering. They further explore persistent three-dimensional features, disentangled shape, viewpoint, and appearance, and output representations ranging from voxel grids and point clouds to continuous occupancy functions and parametric surfaces. Building on these ideas, this work investigates a learned image-to-3D framework that couples two-dimensional observations with an explicit three-dimensional representation and uses image formation constraints to train or refine reconstruction without requiring complete 3D annotations. The framework is intended to support single-view inference while incorporating additional views when available, and to produce detailed geometry suitable for novel-view synthesis and surface recovery. Across object and natural-image settings, the results indicate that imposing projective and multi-view consistency improves reconstruction and generalization, while representations focused on surfaces or continuous functions provide greater resolution and efficiency than dense volumetric predictions.

original_abstract: AI Ethics is now a global topic of discussion in academic and policy circles. At least 84 public-private initiatives have produced statements describing high-level principles, values, and other tenets to guide the ethical development, deployment, and governance of AI. According to recent meta-analyses, AI Ethics has seemingly converged on a set of principles that closely resemble the four classic principles of medical ethics. Despite the initial credibility granted to a principled approach to AI Ethics by the connection to principles in medical ethics, there are reasons to be concerned about its future impact on AI development and governance. Significant differences exist between medicine and AI development that suggest a principled approach in the latter may not enjoy success comparable to the former. Compared to medicine, AI development lacks (1) common aims and fiduciary duties, (2) professional history and norms, (3) proven methods to translate principles into practice, and (4) robust legal and professional accountability mechanisms. These differences suggest we should not yet celebrate consensus around high-level principles that hide deep political and normative disagreement.
generated_abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly mediates decisions with significant consequences for individuals, organizations, and democratic societies. Although ethical principles and guidelines have proliferated, substantial disagreement remains about their meaning, scope, and implementation, while machine-learning systems introduce technical, organizational, and institutional forms of opacity. The resulting gap between what ethical AI should achieve and how it can be developed and governed is compounded by limited evidence that codes of conduct or abstract principles change practitioners’ decisions. Building on analyses of algorithmic ethics, global guidelines, ethical frameworks, and the experiences of industry practitioners, we examine how ethical commitments can be translated into actionable practices across the machine-learning lifecycle. We propose an approach that connects principles such as transparency, justice and fairness, non-maleficence, responsibility, and privacy with context-sensitive assessment, development, and governance, while recognizing the limits of purely technical solutions. We further argue that consequential challenges cannot be left to voluntary ethics alone and may require enforceable rules, democratic accountability, and human-rights safeguards. Ethical AI therefore depends not on consensus statements in isolation, but on implementation strategies that assign responsibility and support informed, critical decision-making in practice.

original_abstract: This paper develops several average-case reduction techniques to show new hardness results for three central high-dimensional statistics problems, implying a statistical-computational gap induced by robustness, a detection-recovery gap and a universality principle for these gaps. A main feature of our approach is to map to these problems via a common intermediate problem that we introduce, which we call Imbalanced Sparse Gaussian Mixtures. We assume the planted clique conjecture for a version of the planted clique problem where the position of the planted clique is mildly constrained, and from this obtain the following computational lower bounds: (1) a $k$-to-$k^2$ statistical-computational gap for robust sparse mean estimation, providing the first average-case evidence for a conjecture of Li (2017) and Balakrishnan et al. (2017); (2) a tight lower bound for semirandom planted dense subgraph, which shows that a semirandom adversary shifts the detection threshold in planted dense subgraph to the conjectured recovery threshold; and (3) a universality principle for $k$-to-$k^2$ gaps in a broad class of sparse mixture problems that includes many natural formulations such as the spiked covariance model. #R##N#Our main approach is to introduce several average-case techniques to produce structured and Gaussianized versions of an input graph problem, and then to rotate these high-dimensional Gaussians by matrices carefully constructed from hyperplanes in $\mathbb{F}_r^t$. For our universality result, we introduce a new method to perform an algorithmic change of measure tailored to sparse mixtures. We also provide evidence that the mild promise in our variant of planted clique does not change the complexity of the problem.
generated_abstract: We study the gap between information-theoretic and computational limits in high-dimensional inference with planted sparse structure. original_abstract: The desire to map neural networks to varying-capacity devices has led to the development of a wealth of compression techniques, many of which involve replacing standard convolutional blocks in a large network with cheap alternative blocks. However, not all blocks are created equally; for a required compute budget there may exist a potent combination of many different cheap blocks, though exhaustively searching for such a combination is prohibitively expensive. In this work, we develop BlockSwap: a fast algorithm for choosing networks with interleaved block types by passing a single minibatch of training data through randomly initialised networks and gauging their Fisher potential. These networks can then be used as students and distilled with the original large network as a teacher. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the chosen networks across CIFAR-10 and ImageNet for classification, and COCO for detection, and provide a comprehensive ablation study of our approach. BlockSwap quickly explores possible block configurations using a simple architecture ranking system, yielding highly competitive networks in orders of magnitude less time than most architecture search techniques (e.g. under 5 minutes on a single GPU for CIFAR-10). Code is available at https://github.com/BayesWatch/pytorch-blockswap.
generated_abstract: Modern deep neural networks achieve strong visual recognition performance but contain substantial redundancy, resulting in excessive parameter storage, computation, and memory traffic. Residual architectures further provide a strong basis for efficient networks, while increasing width rather than depth can improve both optimization and efficiency. Building on these observations, we formulate a sparsity-oriented approach that selects or retains only task-relevant parameters and connections, while preserving the representational benefits of residual and densely connected designs. The available evidence supports the conclusion that substantial reductions in parameters, floating-point operations, and memory access are possible with little or no loss in recognition accuracy. It does not determine a more specific algorithm, architecture, or quantitative result for the present study.

original_abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of generating a set ofrealistic and diverse backgrounds when given only a smallforeground region. We refer to this task as image outpaint-ing. The technical challenge of this task is to synthesize notonly plausible but also diverse image outputs. Traditionalgenerative adversarial networks suffer from mode collapse.While recent approaches propose to maximize orpreserve the pairwise distance between generated sampleswith respect to their latent distance, they do not explicitlyprevent the diverse samples of different conditional inputsfrom collapsing. Therefore, we propose a new regulariza-tion method to encourage diverse sampling in conditionalsynthesis. In addition, we propose a feature pyramid dis-criminator to improve the image quality. Our experimen-tal results show that our model can produce more diverseimages without sacrificing visual quality compared to state-of-the-arts approaches in both the CelebA face dataset and the Cityscape scene dataset.
generated_abstract: Generating realistic images with controllable content remains challenging: synthesized objects must agree with their surroundings in geometry, appearance, structure, and semantics, while outputs should remain sharp and diverse.
