Building on these ideas, we study conditional image synthesis and editing in which available visual context and semantic information guide the generation of missing or newly inserted content. Our approach combines a generative network with adversarial and perceptual objectives, allowing it to infer plausible structures, borrow compatible appearance cues from the surrounding image, and produce realistic details without restricting the location or extent of the generated region. The formulation also supports multiple valid outputs for the same context, reflecting the inherent ambiguity of visual completion. Experiments on image generation, inpainting, and object insertion demonstrate that the proposed framework produces more coherent structures, sharper textures, and improved semantic consistency than approaches based solely on pixel reconstruction or unconstrained synthesis. These results show that context-aware adversarial generation is a practical foundation for realistic and controllable image manipulation.

original_abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) is one of the best methods for understanding the differences in semantic rules between two languages. Especially for Indo-European languages, subword-level models have achieved impressive results. However, when the translation task involves Chinese, semantic granularity remains at the word and character level, so there is still need more fine-grained translation model of Chinese. In this paper, we introduce a simple and effective method for Chinese translation at the sub-character level. Our approach uses the Wubi method to translate Chinese into English; byte-pair encoding (BPE) is then applied. Our method for Chinese-English translation eliminates the need for a complicated word segmentation algorithm during preprocessing. Furthermore, our method allows for sub-character-level neural translation based on recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture, without preprocessing. The empirical results show that for Chinese-English translation tasks, our sub-character-level model has a comparable BLEU score to the subword model, despite having a much smaller vocabulary. Additionally, the small vocabulary is highly advantageous for NMT model compression.
generated_abstract: Neural machine translation must translate an effectively unbounded set of word forms, yet conventional systems rely on fixed vocabularies and therefore struggle with rare words, unknown words, and morphologically rich languages. Word-level encoder–decoder models also depend on explicit segmentation and may lose information when a source sentence is compressed into a fixed-length representation. We address these limitations by combining attention-based translation with representations that expose character and subword structure. Words can be decomposed into subword units, while character-based components provide representations for unseen source forms and generate well-formed target words when required. This design retains the efficiency of word- or subword-level translation while allowing open-vocabulary behavior, and it is compatible with convolutional, recurrent, and hybrid word-character architectures. We further consider character-level decoding without explicit segmentation and reversible encodings for languages whose writing systems differ substantially. The resulting framework exploits copying, transliteration, compounding, and morphological regularities rather than relying on dictionary back-off. Across translation tasks, character and subword information improves robustness to rare forms while preserving competitive translation quality and practical trainability.

original_abstract: While cutting-edge image captioning systems are increasingly describing an image coherently and exactly, recent progresses in continual learning allow deep learning systems to avoid catastrophic forgetting. However, the domain where image captioning working with continual learning is not exploited yet. We define the task in which we consolidate continual learning and image captioning as continual image captioning. In this work, we propose ContCap, a framework continually generating captions over a series of new tasks coming, seamlessly integrating continual learning into image captioning accompanied by tackling catastrophic forgetting. After proving catastrophic forgetting in image captioning, we employ freezing, knowledge distillation, and pseudo-labeling techniques to overcome the forgetting dilemma with the baseline is a simple fine-tuning scheme. We split MS-COCO 2014 dataset to perform experiments on incremental tasks without revisiting dataset of previously provided tasks. The experiments are designed to increase the degree of catastrophic forgetting and appraise the capacity of approaches. Experimental results show remarkable improvements in the performance on the old tasks, while the figure for the new task remains almost the same compared to fine-tuning. For example, pseudo-labeling increases CIDEr from 0.287 to 0.576 on the old task and 0.686 down to 0.657 BLEU1 on the new task.
generated_abstract: We address continual visual learning for image captioning, where a model must acquire new visual concepts and improve its descriptions over time while preserving previously learned recognition and language-generation capabilities. We build on convolutional image captioning, which avoids the sequential computation of recurrent language models, and on Neural Baby Talk, which explicitly grounds generated sentences in detected entities. We further draw on incremental-learning strategies based on distillation, exemplars, generative replay, architectural expansion, and parameter regularization, including Learning without Forgetting, iCaRL, GEM, and synaptic intelligence. Our approach therefore combines an image-captioning architecture with mechanisms that retain prior predictions or representations while learning from newly available data, supporting incremental acquisition of object concepts and their associated language. The resulting formulation is intended to preserve old captioning behavior, incorporate novel objects and scenes, and remain suitable for repeated updates. The cited evidence determines the need for such a unified continual captioning setting and motivates this general solution, but does not specify the paper’s particular implementation or quantitative conclusions.

original_abstract: Recent advancements in machine learning research, i.e., deep learning, introduced methods that excel conventional algorithms as well as humans in several complex tasks, ranging from detection of objects in images and speech recognition to playing difficult strategic games. However, the current methodology of machine learning research and consequently, implementations of the real-world applications of such algorithms, seems to have a recurring HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known) issue. In this work, we elaborate on the algorithmic, economic and social reasons and consequences of this phenomenon. We present examples from current common practices of conducting machine learning research (e.g. avoidance of reporting negative results) and failure of generalization ability of the proposed algorithms and datasets in actual real-life usage. Furthermore, a potential future trajectory of machine learning research and development from the perspective of accountable, unbiased, ethical and privacy-aware algorithmic decision making is discussed. We would like to emphasize that with this discussion we neither claim to provide an exhaustive argumentation nor blame any specific institution or individual on the raised issues. This is simply a discussion put forth by us, insiders of the machine learning field, reflecting on us.
generated_abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) has emerged as a means of reducing the human effort required to design neural networks, using reinforcement learning, evolutionary algorithms, sequential model-based optimization, and random search to explore architecture spaces. However, reported gains are difficult to interpret: comparisons often confound search strategy with computational budget, candidate evaluation, weight sharing, and repeated use of benchmark test sets. We examine NAS as a search problem rather than judging it solely by the accuracy of a final selected model. Our analysis compares learned search policies with random selection and considers the effects of early stopping, shared weights, reproducibility, and evaluation on newly collected data. We further distinguish the quality of the search from the quality of the resulting architecture, and discuss why benchmark improvements need not establish robust generalization or meaningful interpretability. The evidence indicates that several prominent NAS procedures can perform no better than simple baselines, that weight sharing can distort architecture rankings, and that published results may be sensitive to experimental choices. Reliable progress therefore requires explicit search-phase evaluation, repeated and reproducible experiments, and validation beyond repeatedly reused test sets.

original_abstract: One of the primary challenges faced by deep learning is the degree to which current methods exploit superficial statistics and dataset bias, rather than learning to generalise over the specific representations they have experienced. This is a critical concern because generalisation enables robust reasoning over unseen data, whereas leveraging superficial statistics is fragile to even small changes in data distribution. To illuminate the issue and drive progress towards a solution, we propose a test that explicitly evaluates abstract reasoning over visual data. We introduce a large-scale benchmark of visual questions that involve operations fundamental to many high-level vision tasks, such as comparisons of counts and logical operations on complex visual properties. The benchmark directly measures a method's ability to infer high-level relationships and to generalise them over image-based concepts. It includes multiple training/test splits that require controlled levels of generalization. We evaluate a range of deep learning architectures, and find that existing models, including those popular for vision-and-language tasks, are unable to solve seemingly-simple instances. Models using relational networks fare better but leave substantial room for improvement.
generated_abstract: Visual Question Answering (VQA) requires an agent to combine visual understanding, language comprehension, and reasoning to answer natural-language questions about images. Although existing systems achieve strong benchmark performance, their reliance on dataset biases, monolithic representations, and limited answer vocabularies can obscure weaknesses in compositional reasoning and generalization. We review approaches that connect visual and textual modalities through convolutional and recurrent networks, attention, structured scene and question graphs, memory-augmented and modular architectures, semantic embeddings, retrieval, and meta-learning. We further examine free-form VQA, Visual Dialog, Zero-Shot VQA, TDIUC, CLEVR, and datasets designed to measure abstract reasoning, emphasizing how their question types, annotations, and evaluation protocols expose different capabilities. Building on this analysis, we propose viewing progress in VQA through complementary tests of grounding, structured reasoning, compositionality, open-ended answering, and adaptation to unseen questions and answers, rather than through aggregate accuracy alone. Our synthesis shows that structured representations and carefully designed diagnostics improve interpretability and reveal deficiencies masked by conventional benchmarks. Robust VQA therefore requires evaluation and models that support systematic generalization, explicit reasoning, and interaction with visual and linguistic structure.

original_abstract: In this paper, we propose a Dual Focal Loss (DFL) function, as a replacement for the standard cross entropy (CE) function to achieve a better treatment of the unbalanced classes in a dataset. Our DFL method is an improvement on the recently reported Focal Loss (FL) cross-entropy function, which proposes a scaling method that puts more weight on the examples that are difficult to classify over those that are easy. However, the scaling parameter of FL is empirically set, which is problem-dependent. In addition, like other CE variants, FL only focuses on the loss of true classes. Therefore, no loss feedback is gained from the false classes. Although focusing only on true examples increases probability on true classes and correspondingly reduces probability on false classes due to the nature of the softmax function, it does not achieve the best convergence due to avoidance of the loss on false classes. Our DFL method improves on the simple FL in two ways. Firstly, it takes the idea of FL to focus more on difficult examples than the easy ones, but evaluates loss on both true and negative classes with equal importance. Secondly, the scaling parameter of DFL has been made learnable so that it can tune itself by backpropagation rather than being dependent on manual tuning. In this way, our proposed DFL method offers an auto-tunable loss function that can reduce the class imbalance effect as well as put more focus on both true difficult examples and negative easy examples. Experimental results show that our proposed method provides better accuracy in every test run conducted over a variety of different network models and datasets.
generated_abstract: Accurate and efficient segmentation of brain tumors in magnetic resonance images is challenging because glioblastomas may occur anywhere in the brain and vary substantially in shape, size, and contrast. The problem is further complicated by severe class imbalance and the need to recover precise tumor boundaries. We develop a fully convolutional neural network for pixel-wise brain-tumor segmentation, building on convolutional models that combine deep contextual representations with fine spatial information. The network uses an encoder-decoder design with skip connections to preserve localization, while multi-scale features and learned upsampling support segmentation of tumors with varying appearance and extent. To address the dominance of non-tumor labels, we employ a loss formulation based on hierarchical Dice objectives, treating the containing relationships among tumor classes through multiple binary decisions. We also consider architectural refinements, including additional connections and an expanded decoder, and efficient convolutional designs that reduce computational and memory demands. Experiments on brain-tumor MR-image data show that the resulting framework improves the balance between region accuracy and boundary localization, achieves competitive Dice, precision, recall, and intersection-over-union scores, and provides a practical alternative to earlier fully convolutional approaches.

original_abstract: Given an artistic portrait, recovering the latent photorealistic face that preserves the subject’s identity is challenging because the facial details are often distorted or fully lost in artistic portraits. We develop an Identity-preserving Face Recovery from Portraits method that utilizes a Style Removal network (SRN) and a Discriminative Network (DN). Our SRN, composed of an autoencoder with residual block-embedded skip connections, is designed to transfer feature maps of stylized images to the feature maps of the corresponding photorealistic faces. Owing to the Spatial Transformer Network, SRN automatically compensates for misalignments of stylized portraits to output aligned realistic face images. To ensure the identity preservation, we promote the recovered and ground truth faces to share similar visual features via a distance measure which compares features of recovered and ground truth faces extracted from a pre-trained FaceNet network. DN has multiple convolutional and fully-connected layers, and its role is to enforce recovered faces to be similar to authentic faces. Thus, we can recover high-quality photorealistic faces from unaligned portraits while preserving the identity of the face in an image. By conducting extensive evaluations on a large-scale synthesized dataset and a hand-drawn sketch dataset, we demonstrate that our method achieves superior face recovery and attains state-of-the-art results. In addition, our method can recover photorealistic faces from unseen stylized portraits, artistic paintings, and hand-drawn sketches.
generated_abstract: Neural style transfer addresses the synthesis of an image that preserves the content of one input while reproducing the visual appearance of another. We examine the limitations that have accompanied this goal: iterative optimization is computationally expensive, whereas feed-forward networks may be restricted to predefined styles, produce insufficient diversity, or lose perceptual quality. Building on representations from pretrained convolutional networks, perceptual losses, texture statistics, and feature-normalization strategies, we develop a unified perspective on how content and style are represented and controlled. We organize existing approaches according to their treatment of spatial location, color, scale, local structure, and style interpolation, and discuss the trade-offs among quality, stability, efficiency, generality, and user control. Particular attention is given to methods that replace optimization with learned feed-forward synthesis and to mechanisms that support arbitrary styles and multiple textures. The resulting analysis shows that content and style are not completely separated in deep features, and that improved control and diversity require explicit design rather than a single loss. These observations establish practical directions for efficient, stable, and flexible stylization.

original_abstract: Quantization of neural networks has become common practice, driven by the need for efficient implementations of deep neural networks on embedded devices. In this paper, we exploit an oft-overlooked degree of freedom in most networks - for a given layer, individual output channels can be scaled by any factor provided that the corresponding weights of the next layer are inversely scaled. Therefore, a given network has many factorizations which change the weights of the network without changing its function. We present a conceptually simple and easy to implement method that uses this property and show that proper factorizations significantly decrease the degradation caused by quantization. We show improvement on a wide variety of networks and achieve state-of-the-art degradation results for MobileNets. While our focus is on quantization, this type of factorization is applicable to other domains such as network-pruning, neural nets regularization and network interpretability.
generated_abstract: Deep neural networks deliver high accuracy, but their storage, computation, and energy requirements hinder deployment on embedded and mobile hardware. Limited precision offers a practical route to reduce model size and arithmetic cost, yet quantization can introduce rounding noise, clipping distortion, activation-range errors, and accuracy degradation. This paper studies the conversion of full-precision networks to fixed-point and integer representations, considering both inference and training. It builds on evidence that stochastic rounding, optimized layer bit-width allocation, weight sharing, pruning, retraining, channel-level statistics, analytically selected clipping values, and quantization-aware optimization can preserve accuracy while improving memory use, latency, and energy efficiency. We propose a unified approach that calibrates tensor ranges, assigns suitable precision, and incorporates retraining when necessary, while retaining higher precision only for operations that are especially sensitive to quantization. Experiments across image classification and object detection networks evaluate accuracy, model size, latency, and energy. The results indicate that carefully designed low-precision representations can approach floating-point performance with substantial efficiency gains, and that further reductions require explicit treatment of numerical noise and normalization.

original_abstract: We propose a planning and perception mechanism for a robot (agent), that can only observe the underlying environment partially, in order to solve an image classification problem. A three-layer architecture is suggested that consists of a meta-layer that decides the intermediate goals, an action-layer that selects local actions as the agent navigates towards a goal, and a classification-layer that evaluates the reward and makes a prediction. We design and implement these layers using deep reinforcement learning. A generalized policy gradient algorithm is utilized to learn the parameters of these layers to maximize the expected reward. Our proposed methodology is tested on the MNIST dataset of handwritten digits, which provides us with a level of explainability while interpreting the agent's intermediate goals and course of action.
generated_abstract: Autonomous agents operating in complex visual environments must extract task-relevant information from partial observations, select useful goals, and learn effective behavior despite sparse or delayed feedback. Convolutional representations based on local multilayer processing, residual learning, and dense feature propagation provide increasingly discriminative and efficiently trainable visual features. Reinforcement-learning formulations further support intrinsically motivated exploration, hierarchical goal-directed behavior, and information exchange among multiple mobile agents through decentralized consensus. Attention and saliency mechanisms offer a complementary means of prioritizing relevant regions and stimulus features, while goal reasoning enables agents to deliberate over and self-select objectives in dynamic, uncertain settings. The resulting perspective connects visual perception, action selection, and autonomous goal management rather than treating classification or control as isolated stages. The cited results establish that these ingredients can improve representation learning, exploration, decentralized image classification, attentional selection, and autonomous control. They do not, however, determine the specific architecture, task, experimental protocol, or quantitative conclusions of the present work.

original_abstract: While adversarial games have been well studied in various board games and electronic sports games, etc., such adversarial games remain a nearly blank field in natural language processing. As natural language is inherently an interactive game, we propose a challenging pragmatics game called Adversarial Taboo, in which an attacker and a defender compete with each other through sequential natural language interactions. The attacker is tasked with inducing the defender to speak a target word invisible to the defender, while the defender is tasked with detecting the target word before being induced by the attacker. In Adversarial Taboo, a successful attacker must hide its intention and subtly induce the defender, while a competitive defender must be cautious with its utterances and infer the intention of the attacker. To instantiate the game, we create a game environment and a competition platform. Sufficient pilot experiments and empirical studies on several baseline attack and defense strategies show promising and interesting results. Based on the analysis on the game and experiments, we discuss multiple promising directions for future research.
generated_abstract: We investigate how neural agents can learn to communicate effectively when language is used to achieve a shared goal rather than merely to imitate conversational data. Existing dialogue models generate fluent responses but may favor generic utterances, overlook future consequences, and lack explicit reasoning about a partner’s private information, strategy, and knowledge. We build on hierarchical generative dialogue models, diversity-promoting objectives, knowledge-grounded conversation, and reinforcement-learning approaches that encourage informative, coherent, and sustained interaction. We further draw on sequential language games, pragmatic speaker–listener models, negotiation, and collaborative settings in which agents must coordinate through messages while pursuing compatible or partially different objectives. Our approach treats communication as an interactive game and examines the roles of inference, planning, pragmatics, and learned representations in successful coordination. The resulting analysis demonstrates that task incentives and interaction can produce more informative and goal-directed communication than likelihood-based generation alone, while also exposing tensions between communicative success, human interpretability, and natural-language-like behavior. These findings support interactive, multi-agent learning as a useful foundation for developing capable conversational systems.

original_abstract: This paper presents a new model for visual dialog, Recurrent Dual Attention Network (ReDAN), using multi-step reasoning to answer a series of questions about an image. In each question-answering turn of a dialog, ReDAN infers the answer progressively through multiple reasoning steps. In each step of the reasoning process, the semantic representation of the question is updated based on the image and the previous dialog history, and the recurrently-refined representation is used for further reasoning in the subsequent step. On the VisDial v1.0 dataset, the proposed ReDAN model achieves a new state-of-the-art of 64.47% NDCG score. Visualization on the reasoning process further demonstrates that ReDAN can locate context-relevant visual and textual clues via iterative refinement, which can lead to the correct answer step-by-step.
generated_abstract: Visual dialog requires an agent to answer questions about an image while maintaining conversational context and resolving references to previously discussed objects. Unlike image question answering, the relevant visual evidence cannot be determined from the current question alone: the agent must jointly interpret the image, dialog history, question, and candidate answer. We propose an attention-based framework that progressively grounds the question in image regions, exploits relationships between the question and dialog history to resolve ambiguous references, and evaluates answers through their compatibility with the grounded visual and linguistic context. The framework supports both discriminative ranking of candidate responses and generative response production, while retaining interpretable attention that indicates the evidence underlying an answer. Experiments on the Visual Dialog dataset demonstrate that incorporating historical visual attention and answer-aware reasoning improves response selection over approaches that fuse the image, question, and history without explicitly modeling references or the answer. Qualitative analyses further show that attention evolves across dialog turns, locating relevant regions and preserving conversational consistency. These results establish that visual reference resolution and joint image–question–answer reasoning are essential for accurate visual dialog.

original_abstract: Retrieve-and-edit based approaches to structured prediction, where structures associated with retrieved neighbors are edited to form new structures, have recently attracted increased interest. However, much recent work merely conditions on retrieved structures (e.g., in a sequence-to-sequence framework), rather than explicitly manipulating them. We show we can perform accurate sequence labeling by explicitly (and only) copying labels from retrieved neighbors. Moreover, because this copying is label-agnostic, we can achieve impressive performance in zero-shot sequence-labeling tasks. We additionally consider a dynamic programming approach to sequence labeling in the presence of retrieved neighbors, which allows for controlling the number of distinct (copied) segments used to form a prediction, and leads to both more interpretable and accurate predictions.
generated_abstract: Named entity recognition and sequence tagging systems often depend on task-specific features, language resources, and substantial annotated data, making them difficult to apply across domains and languages. We address this problem by combining end-to-end sequence labeling with transfer learning from large amounts of unlabeled text and from related annotated tasks. Building on character- and word-level representations, bidirectional recurrent sequence taggers, and conditional random fields, we use deep bidirectional contextual representations to encode both the meaning of a token and its linguistic context. The resulting representations are incorporated into a sequence tagger with minimal task-specific modification, allowing the model to be fine-tuned for named entity recognition and related tagging tasks. The approach also supports transfer between domains and languages when supervision is limited, without relying on handcrafted features or extensive preprocessing. Experiments demonstrate that contextual pre-training and hierarchical transfer provide substantial improvements over conventional word and character representations, particularly in low-resource and noisy settings. These results show that a general neural architecture can reduce dependence on linguistic knowledge while retaining the structured predictions required for accurate sequence labeling.

original_abstract: We present a comprehensive analysis of how and why face recognition accuracy differs between men and women. We show that accuracy is lower for women due to the combination of (1) the impostor distribution for women having a skew toward higher similarity scores, and (2) the genuine distribution for women having a skew toward lower similarity scores. We show that this phenomenon of the impostor and genuine distributions for women shifting closer towards each other is general across datasets of African-American, Caucasian, and Asian faces. We show that the distribution of facial expressions may differ between male/female, but that the accuracy difference persists for image subsets rated confidently as neutral expression. The accuracy difference also persists for image subsets rated as close to zero pitch angle. Even when removing images with forehead partially occluded by hair/hat, the same impostor/genuine accuracy difference persists. We show that the female genuine distribution improves when only female images without facial cosmetics are used, but that the female impostor distribution also degrades at the same time. Lastly, we show that the accuracy difference persists even if a state-of-the-art deep learning method is trained from scratch using training data explicitly balanced between male and female images and subjects.
generated_abstract: Deep face recognition has achieved high accuracy through large-scale training data and discriminative objectives, yet performance can vary substantially with age and other image covariates. In particular, the behavior of modern systems across age groups remains insufficiently understood, and improvements on unconstrained benchmarks do not by themselves establish equitable recognition. We study this problem by evaluating deep convolutional face matchers under age variation and by examining genuine and impostor score distributions rather than verification rates alone. Building on angular and cosine-margin objectives, including SphereFace, CosFace, and ArcFace, we consider how feature discrimination interacts with training data drawn from MS-Celeb-1M and VGGFace2, whose differences in scale, pose, and age coverage may affect generalization. We further relate age effects to covariates known to influence unconstrained verification. Our analysis is designed to distinguish deficiencies caused by data imbalance from those intrinsic to the learned representation, and to assess whether additional or age-balanced training data reliably improves recognition. The results indicate that strong deep face recognition performance does not remove age-related disparities; older faces remain more difficult to recognize, and increasing their representation alone is not sufficient to resolve the problem.

original_abstract: We propose an unsupervised strategy for the selection of justification sentences for multi-hop question answering (QA) that (a) maximizes the relevance of the selected sentences, (b) minimizes the overlap between the selected facts, and (c) maximizes the coverage of both question and answer. This unsupervised sentence selection method can be coupled with any supervised QA approach. We show that the sentences selected by our method improve the performance of a state-of-the-art supervised QA model on two multi-hop QA datasets: AI2's Reasoning Challenge (ARC) and Multi-Sentence Reading Comprehension (MultiRC). We obtain new state-of-the-art performance on both datasets among approaches that do not use external resources for training the QA system: 56.82\% F1 on ARC (41.24\% on Challenge and 64.49\% on Easy) and 26.1\% EM0 on MultiRC. Our justification sentences have higher quality than the justifications selected by a strong information retrieval baseline, e.g., by 5.4\% F1 in MultiRC. We also show that our unsupervised selection of justification sentences is more stable across domains than a state-of-the-art supervised sentence selection method.
generated_abstract: Open-domain question answering increasingly requires reasoning over evidence distributed across multiple passages rather than extracting an answer from a single document. Retrieved text contains irrelevant and conflicting information, while existing reading-comprehension systems often select answer candidates independently and struggle to identify the evidence chain needed for multi-hop inference. We address this problem by integrating document retrieval, answer extraction, and evidence reasoning in a unified question-answering framework. The approach represents textual evidence and entity mentions across passages, identifies relevant sentences, aggregates support for competing answer candidates, and uses cross-passage verification to select an answer consistent with the available evidence. It further exploits entailment signals and semantic structure to distinguish useful facts from distractors and to support explainable predictions through sentence-level supporting facts. Experiments on multi-hop and open-domain question-answering benchmarks, including Wikipedia-based tasks, demonstrate that reasoning across documents substantially improves over independent passage readers and answer reranking based on isolated evidence. The results show that selecting and combining relevant information remains as important as answer span prediction, and that explicit evidence aggregation provides a practical path toward more accurate and interpretable multi-hop question answering.
